title: Diffusion Models and Image Generation
summary: Diffusion models generate images by learning to reverse a process that gradually adds noise, starting from random noise and denoising into a coherent image guided by a text prompt. They power tools like Stable Diffusion and are essential for the visu
content:
# Diffusion Models and Image Generation ##### The ₹40,000 photoshoot that became a ₹12 prompt A small apparel brand in Tiruppur used to spend around ₹40,000 per product photoshoot — studio hire, model, photographer, lighting, editing, and a two-week turnaround for a catalogue of thirty items. In 2024 their designer started generating lifestyle backgrounds with Stable Diffusion and compositing the real garment photographs onto them. Studio cost dropped to a plain white cyclorama shoot. Backgrounds — a Goa beach at golden hour, a Mumbai rooftop at dusk, a Jaipur courtyard — cost a few rupees of GPU time each and arrived in ninety seconds. The garment is always real, because customers must see the actual product. The *world around it* is generated. That distinction is worth holding onto. Diffusion models are not a replacement for photography; they are a new tool with specific strengths, specific failure modes, and real ethical questions. Understanding how they work is what lets you use them well — and it also completes your picture of generative AI, because everything so far has been about text. ##### The core idea Here is the insight, and it is genuinely elegant. Generating a coherent image from nothing is extraordinarily hard. But **removing a small amount of noise from a slightly noisy image is easy** — and you can create unlimited training data for it by simply adding noise to real photographs. So: train a network to denoise a little. Then apply it repeatedly, starting from pure noise. Each step removes a bit of noise, and after enough steps you have an image. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph FWD["Forward process — training data, no learning"] A["Real image"] -->|"+ noise"| B["t=200"] B -->|"+ noise"| C["t=500"] C -->|"+ noise"| D["t=800"] D -->|"+ noise"| E["Pure noise
t=1000"] end subgraph REV["Reverse process — what the model learns"] F["Pure noise"] -->|"predict & remove noise"| G["t=800"] G -->|"denoise"| H["t=500"] H -->|"denoise"| I["t=200"] I -->|"denoise"| J["Generated image"] end K["Text prompt"] -.guides every step.-> REV ``` ##### The forward process The forward process adds Gaussian noise on a fixed schedule. It involves no learning at all — it is just a recipe for generating training pairs. $$q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}\left(x_t; \sqrt{1-\beta_t}\, x_{t-1}, \beta_t \mathbf{I}\right)$$ The useful property, from Ho et al.'s 2020 DDPM paper, is that you can jump to any timestep in one step: $$x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}\, \epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I})$$ where $\bar{\alpha}_t = \prod_{s=1}^{t}(1 - \beta_s)$. ```python import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt T = 1000 betas = np.linspace(1e-4, 0.02, T) # linear noise schedule alphas = 1.0 - betas alpha_bar = np.cumprod(alphas) def add_noise(x0, t, rng=np.random.default_rng(0)): """Jump straight to timestep t.""" eps = rng.standard_normal(x0.shape) return (np.sqrt(alpha_bar[t]) * x0 + np.sqrt(1 - alpha_bar[t]) * eps), eps image = plt.imread("garment.png")[..., :3] fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(15, 3.2)) for ax, t in zip(axes, [0, 200, 500, 800, 999]): noisy, _ = add_noise(image, t) ax.imshow(np.clip(noisy, 0, 1)); ax.set_title(f"t={t}"); ax.axis("off") ``` Run that and you can watch a photograph dissolve into static. Every intermediate frame is a training example: input the noisy image and `t`, target the noise that was added. ##### The reverse process The model — a **U-Net** — takes a noisy image and a timestep, and predicts the noise. Subtract the prediction (with the right scaling) and you have a slightly cleaner image. Training is remarkably simple: ```python # Conceptual training loop for batch in dataloader: x0 = batch["images"] t = torch.randint(0, T, (x0.shape[0],)) noise = torch.randn_like(x0) x_t = sqrt_alpha_bar[t] * x0 + sqrt_one_minus_alpha_bar[t] * noise predicted_noise = unet(x_t, t, text_embedding) loss = F.mse_loss(predicted_noise, noise) # ← that's the whole objective loss.backward(); optimizer.step(); optimizer.zero_grad() ``` **Mean squared error on predicted noise.** That is the entire training objective for a system that generates photorealistic images. The complexity lives in the architecture and the scale, not the loss. The U-Net is a convolutional encoder-decoder with skip connections — Day 17's CNN concepts, plus cross-attention layers (Day 21) that inject the text conditioning at multiple resolutions. ##### Latent diffusion Running diffusion in pixel space is prohibitively expensive: a 512×512 RGB image is 786,432 dimensions, and you need 50+ forward passes per generation. **Stable Diffusion's** contribution (Rombach et al., 2022) was to run diffusion in a compressed **latent space** instead. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Text prompt"] --> B["CLIP text encoder"] B --> C["Text embedding
77 × 768"] D["Random noise
64 × 64 × 4"] --> E["U-Net
denoise × N steps"] C -.cross-attention.-> E E --> F["Clean latent
64 × 64 × 4"] F --> G["VAE decoder"] G --> H["Image
512 × 512 × 3"] ``` A VAE compresses 512×512×3 = 786,432 values into 64×64×4 = 16,384 — a **48× reduction**. Diffusion happens in that small space; the decoder expands the result back to pixels. This is why Stable Diffusion runs on a consumer GPU and why image generation became accessible rather than a datacentre operation. ##### Using the Diffusers library ```python import torch from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline, DPMSolverMultistepScheduler pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained( "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-2-1-base", torch_dtype=torch.float16, safety_checker=None, # keep enabled in production ) pipe = pipe.to("cuda") pipe.scheduler = DPMSolverMultistepScheduler.from_config(pipe.scheduler.config) pipe.enable_attention_slicing() # lower VRAM generator = torch.Generator("cuda").manual_seed(42) image = pipe( prompt=("editorial fashion photograph, cotton kurta on a mannequin, " "Jaipur haveli courtyard, golden hour light, shallow depth of field, " "85mm lens, high detail"), negative_prompt=("blurry, distorted hands, extra limbs, watermark, text, " "low quality, oversaturated"), num_inference_steps=30, guidance_scale=7.5, height=512, width=512, generator=generator, ).images[0] image.save("kurta_courtyard.png") ``` ##### The parameters that matter **`guidance_scale` (CFG)** controls how strongly the output follows the prompt. Classifier-free guidance runs the model twice per step — once with the prompt, once without — and extrapolates away from the unconditioned prediction: $$\epsilon_{\text{guided}} = \epsilon_{\text{uncond}} + s \cdot (\epsilon_{\text{cond}} - \epsilon_{\text{uncond}})$$ | Value | Effect | |---|---| | 1.0 | Prompt effectively ignored | | 3–5 | Loose adherence, more creative and varied | | **7–9** | **Balanced — the standard range** | | 12–20 | Rigid adherence, often oversaturated and artefact-heavy | **`num_inference_steps`** is the number of denoising iterations. With a modern scheduler like DPM-Solver++, 20–30 steps is usually indistinguishable from 50. The old DDPM sampler needed 1,000. Scheduler improvements, not model changes, are what made generation fast. **`seed`** makes generation reproducible. Fix the seed while iterating on a prompt, so you are comparing prompt changes rather than random variation. This is the single most useful habit for prompt iteration. **`negative_prompt`** specifies what to avoid. Unlike text LLMs — where Day 30 warned that negation backfires — negative prompts work well here, because they are implemented as a genuine second conditioning signal that guidance pushes *away* from, not as an instruction the model must interpret. ##### Prompting for images Image prompts are descriptive rather than instructional. A useful structure: ``` [subject] [action/pose], [setting], [lighting], [style], [camera/lens], [quality] ``` ```python prompts = { "weak": "a woman wearing a saree", "better": ("portrait of a woman in a red Kanjeevaram silk saree, standing in " "a Chettinad courtyard, warm afternoon light through a doorway, " "editorial photography, 85mm f/1.8, shallow depth of field, " "fine fabric detail"), } ``` Elements that reliably help: **medium** (photograph, oil painting, 3D render), **lighting** (golden hour, softbox, rim lighting), **camera** (35mm, macro, wide-angle), **composition** (close-up, aerial, rule of thirds), and **mood**. Prompt weighting is supported in many pipelines: `(silk texture:1.4)` increases emphasis, `(background:0.6)` decreases it. ##### Image-to-image and inpainting **Image-to-image** starts from your image rather than pure noise: ```python from diffusers import StableDiffusionImg2ImgPipeline from PIL import Image pipe = StableDiffusionImg2ImgPipeline.from_pretrained( "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-2-1-base", torch_dtype=torch.float16 ).to("cuda") init = Image.open("sketch.png").convert("RGB").resize((512, 512)) result = pipe( prompt="detailed product photograph of a leather handbag, studio lighting", image=init, strength=0.6, # 0 = unchanged, 1 = ignores the input entirely guidance_scale=7.5, num_inference_steps=30, ).images[0] ``` `strength` sets how much noise is added before denoising begins. **0.3–0.5 preserves composition and restyles; 0.7–0.9 keeps only loose structure.** **Inpainting** regenerates a masked region — this is the Tiruppur workflow: ```python from diffusers import StableDiffusionInpaintPipeline pipe = StableDiffusionInpaintPipeline.from_pretrained( "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-2-inpainting", torch_dtype=torch.float16 ).to("cuda") result = pipe( prompt="Goa beach at sunset, soft warm light, blurred palm trees", image=product_photo, mask_image=background_mask, # white = regenerate, black = keep num_inference_steps=30, guidance_scale=8.0, ).images[0] ``` Related techniques worth knowing: **ControlNet** conditions generation on pose, depth, edges, or a scribble, giving precise structural control. **LoRA for diffusion** — the same technique from Day 29 — lets you teach a specific style or product with 20–30 images. **DreamBooth** teaches a specific subject. ##### Limitations and ethics Being honest about what these models get wrong: - **Text in images** is usually garbled, though newer models have improved. - **Hands and fingers** — the canonical failure, caused by high anatomical variability in training data. - **Counting.** "Five apples" reliably produces four or six. - **Spatial relations.** "The cup to the left of the book" is often ignored. - **Consistency across generations.** The same character in two images will differ without LoRA or a reference technique. The ethical questions are real and unsettled: - **Training data consent.** These models trained on billions of scraped images, mostly without permission. Multiple lawsuits are ongoing. - **Style imitation.** Prompting an artist's name reproduces their style without compensation. - **Deepfakes.** Generating identifiable real people, especially in misleading contexts, is harmful and increasingly regulated. - **Bias.** Prompt "a doctor" or "a CEO" and observe the demographic skew — the training data's biases are reproduced faithfully. - **Disclosure.** Label AI-generated imagery. India's IT Rules amendments and the EU AI Act both push toward mandatory disclosure, and it is the right practice regardless. Day 42's governance material applies directly here. ##### Common mistakes - **`guidance_scale` above 15**, producing oversaturated, artefact-heavy images. - **50+ steps** with a modern scheduler, wasting time for no visible gain. - **Not fixing the seed** while iterating, so you cannot tell prompt changes from randomness. - **No negative prompt** — it is cheap and usually helps. - **Prompts too short.** "A cat" gives you a generic cat; detail is what produces quality. - **`float32` on GPU** when `float16` halves memory at no visible quality cost. - **Wrong resolution for the base model.** SD 1.5 was trained at 512×512 and degrades outside it; SDXL at 1024×1024. - **`strength=1.0` in img2img**, which discards your input entirely. - **Disabling the safety checker in production.** - **Not disclosing AI-generated images.** - **Expecting accurate text rendering** or reliable counting. ##### Hands-on: sweep the parameters Your practical task generates images and experiments with guidance scale and steps. Do it as a grid: fix the seed and the prompt, then vary `guidance_scale` across 3, 7, 12, and 18, and `num_inference_steps` across 10, 20, 30, and 50. Save all sixteen and view them together. You will see quality plateau around 25–30 steps and images become harsh above guidance 12 — and those two observations will set your defaults for every project after this. The mini project is a text-to-image web app with prompt controls and img2img editing. Gradio makes this quick, and it is a strong portfolio piece because it is visual. Expose seed, guidance, steps, and negative prompt as controls, and — important for usability — display the seed of every generated image so users can reproduce one they liked. Add an img2img tab with a `strength` slider so people can feel what that parameter does. The assignment explains forward and reverse diffusion with text conditioning. Include the noise-schedule visualisation from earlier — showing an actual image dissolving over timesteps makes the forward process concrete in a way equations do not. Then explain that the model learns to predict the added noise, that generation applies this repeatedly from pure noise, and that cross-attention on CLIP text embeddings steers each step. Close with why latent diffusion made it 48× cheaper. ##### Key takeaways - **Diffusion learns to remove a little noise**, then applies that repeatedly from pure noise — the training objective is simply MSE on predicted noise. - **The forward process is a fixed recipe with no learning**, which is what gives you unlimited training pairs from any image collection. - **Latent diffusion runs the process in a 48× compressed space**, which is why Stable Diffusion fits on a consumer GPU. - **Guidance scale 7–9 and 20–30 steps with a modern scheduler** are the defaults, and fixing the seed is what makes prompt iteration a controlled experiment. - **Know the failure modes and the ethics** — hands, text, and counting fail; training-data consent, style imitation, deepfakes, and disclosure are live issues you are responsible for.
